claims.text: Wear resistance of HEA coatings on transition-metal matrices improves as ambient temperature rises from room temperature to approximately 400 °C.
The improvement up to approximately 400 °C is caused by adaptive, self-lubricating oxide tribo-layers.
Above approximately 400 °C, wear performance degrades rapidly because refractory elements oxidize excessively.
High-temperature degradation involves loss of coating structural integrity.
CuMoTaWV is an example of a metallic high-entropy coating system relevant to the hypothesis.
The initial coating has a nanocrystalline or multiphase microstructure with high hardness.
The initial coating contains surface oxides.
Tribological testing of high-entropy coatings has been conducted over temperatures from room temperature to 600 °C.
A 10 N load and 0.18 m/s sliding speed are applicable constant conditions for the proposed elevated-temperature coating tests.
With increasing temperature, the surface tribo-layer changes sequentially from a stable hard oxide to a V-rich or Mo-rich lubricating phase and then to a porous excessive oxide.
At 200–400 °C, thermal activation promotes diffusion of Mo, V, and Cu to the sliding surface.
CuO, MoO3, and V2O5 form a dense self-lubricating layer that reduces friction and wear.
At approximately 400–500 °C, excessive oxidation produces a thick, brittle, and unstable oxide layer.
The brittle oxide layer fractures under sliding shear and produces abrasive debris, delamination, and increased wear.
Wear rate reaches a minimum near 400 °C and then rises sharply above 400 °C.
Above the degradation boundary, coefficient of friction remains low even while wear volume increases significantly.
At room temperature, the coating has relatively high friction because a thermally activated lubricating oxide layer is absent.
The degradation boundary for V-rich HEA systems lies between 400 °C and 500 °C.
The degradation temperature depends on alloy composition, particularly V content, and on the transition-metal matrix.
Absence of degradation in a V-free AlCrFeNiW coating at 450 °C would falsify excessive oxidation of refractory elements as the dominant failure mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism is framed broadly as excessive oxidation of refractory elements, including V or Mo, but the proposed experiment replaces V with another readily oxidizable refractory element, W. Good performance of AlCrFeNiW would challenge a V-specific explanation but would not by itself falsify the broader refractory-element oxidation mechanism.
